Alaska.Ai — Anchorage Desk Draft

2026-08-14 · branch claude/linkedin-desk-2026-08-14

Copy this for LinkedIn

Anchorage Assembly member Keith McCormick led the objection that held up APD’s roughly $600,000 Real-Time Crime Center upgrade on August 4. The binding vote lands August 18.

McCormick represents Eagle River and Chugiak on the Assembly, and the APD system he stalled runs across the whole Anchorage bowl. The desk covered the award side of this contract on August 7. The Assembly side is the harder half.

According to Alaska’s News Source, which reported the meeting on August 5, members declined to approve APD’s three-year contract with Thundercat Technology Inc. and postponed action to the August 18 meeting. That outlet is the only one carrying the August 4 debate in detail, which is worth stating before the analysis rests on it. The Real-Time Crime Center ingests up to 750 camera feeds plus drones, license-plate readers, and object-recognition analytics.

McCormick’s objection, per that account, wasn’t about the cameras. “All the guardrails that you just stated are policy and when my constituents ask, ‘what are we collecting? Who can see it? How long do we keep it?’ Anchorage code can’t answer any of those questions,” he said. The binary he owned was clean. Fund the upgrade now, or withhold until Anchorage Municipal Code sets binding collection, access, and retention rules.

Withholding the money was the right call. What Anchorage is buying is not an AI model. It is the camera, ALPR, drone, and analytics infrastructure that surveillance AI runs on, which is the layer Alaska’s AI oversight conversation keeps skipping. Anchorage barred facial recognition in 2023, so the municipality has proven it can legislate here. On this record it has no binding code governing the object-recognition analytics the Thundercat upgrade would expand. Policy written inside the executive branch can be rewritten inside the executive branch, which is McCormick’s second point. “We have no legislative guardrails. This is an entirely bundling power under the executive branch without any check or balance.”

The counter-case is real. APD frames this as routine public-safety modernization, and a member who trusts the 2023 ban plus the chief’s committee-notification commitments could reasonably approve on August 18 and pursue code separately.

Watch one thing on August 18. Either McCormick converts the objection into a code-level data-governance amendment on collection, access, and retention as a condition of approval, or the Assembly approves the Thundercat contract as written and leaves governance to executive policy. His no vote on the March 2026 data-center zoning ordinance AO 2026-27 suggests he keeps pressing the guardrails-before-infrastructure line.

If you held that seat on August 18, would you condition the Thundercat contract on binding retention and access rules in code, or approve it and legislate the guardrails afterward?

#AlaskaAI #AIPolicy #ProcurementReform

Editor note:
SHIPPED CAVEATED — read this before posting.

1. CORROBORATION DEPTH IS THIN (the main caveat). The validator selected this candidate under the ship-caveated rule at MEDIUM confidence. The detailed account of the August 4 Assembly debate is carried by ONE independent outlet (Alaska's News Source). The MOA Public Health and Safety Committee packet and the Must Read Alaska piece confirm the Thundercat contract and the RTCC's scale, but do not independently reconstruct the debate. The post discloses this limitation in body copy rather than hiding it. Both McCormick quotes were re-verified verbatim on the live primary page.

2. TIME-DECAY CHECK BEFORE YOU POST. The post states that outlet is the only one carrying the August 4 debate in detail. That was accurate at dossier build. If another outlet reconstructs the debate before you publish, that sentence becomes false. Worth thirty seconds of checking on the morning you post.

3. EDITORIAL PROXIMITY — SECOND ISSUE ON ONE CONTRACT. The 2026-08-07 desk post covered this same ~$600,000 Thundercat RTCC contract from the executive side (Chief Sean Case). The dedupe gate is NOT tripped: different subject, different branch of government, different owned binary, different forward hook, and Case is the blocked subject, not McCormick. The editor judged the proximity justified because the analytical content is new in full (the code-versus-policy distinction, the 2023 ban as proof of legislative capacity, the AO 2026-27 voting pattern). The post now acknowledges the prior coverage explicitly so the repetition reads as the desk building rather than forgetting. Verified against the archive: branch claude/linkedin-desk-2026-08-07 does carry the Sean Case dossier.

4. FOUNDERS SLICE RETURNED ZERO. An honest empty, not a stall. The strongest Anchorage-founder AI decisions of 2026 are all already on the permanent blocklist (Kellie/Applied Atomics, Mahoney/Stak), Greensparc is SF-headquartered and fails the Anchorage tie, and the gBETA cohort and Terra Energy fall outside the window.

5. SEARCH POLLUTION — RECOMMEND A SOURCES.YAML BLOCKLIST. The founders scout hit multiple fabricated claims that failed verification against every primary source and explicitly refused to use them: a "Sovereign Sensors $3.5M Series A permafrost AI" round, an "Arctic AI $23M fund", and the aggregator domains dailyanchorage.news, blog.mean.ceo, and nucamp startup roundups. None reached the post. Worth adding an explicit blocklist to config/sources.yaml so future runs discard them earlier.

6. A STRONG LEAD WAS CHASED AND HONESTLY DROPPED. Koniag Technology Solutions won a Department of the Air Force / AFRL task order for an AI/ML attrition-risk and retention solution, awarded 2026-06-22 at $1,243,148.04. Explicitly AI/ML and squarely in window. Dropped because no named human decision owner could be tied to the award, the winning subsidiary is headquartered in Chantilly VA, and the Anchorage tie was unproven. No name was invented to rescue it. If a named Koniag program lead surfaces, this is a strong future candidate.

7. CONFIG DRIFT WORTH FIXING (three files disagree with the routine). The routine now runs a 60-day decision window (90 on broadening) and a 21-day subject-repeat window. But config/desk_rubric.yaml still encodes "last 30 days (45 if broadened)" in its recent_decision hard-fail check, and .claude/agents/desk-scout.md and .claude/agents/desk-validator.md still say 30/45 days and "last 12 issues". All three were overridden in the spawn prompts this run, and the scorer was told to grade the substance rather than the stale number. This works but is fragile. Updating those three files would remove a standing failure mode.

8. TYPOGRAPHIC NORMALIZATION. The writer returned straight quotes; they were converted to curly per brand.yaml. Glyphs only, no wording changed. The dossier stores the quotes with straight glyphs, so a character-level diff of the quoted spans will show that difference. The wording is identical.

9. PROCESS COUNTS. Editor ran 2 of a permitted 3 cycles (revise, then ship). Scorer ran 1 of a permitted 3 and cleared the 8.0 threshold on the first pass at 9.07 with no hard-fail. The scorer's weakest-criterion fix (splitting a dense paragraph) was applied after scoring as a paragraph break only, changing no wording.

10. IMAGE PATH. Built through the alaska-ai-artwork skill (bespoke art), not the alaska-ai-brief template. The repo's SKILL.md now designates the template as emergency fallback only, which supersedes the routine prompt's older instruction. The fallback did NOT fire. Six eval iterations, 6.51 to 8.58 weighted, no dimension below 7, QA check passed at 1080x1080. Style engraved_headworks, hue neutral-cool, composition frame_within, seed 818, all clear of the dedup cooldowns. The artist rejected the orchestrator's suggested patchbay concept as too close to the 2026-08-07 piece's blank-ordinance-page motif and built a stop-log gate headworks instead. Every number on the art (750, $600,000, AUG 18, 2023) traces to the dossier. Weakest dimension was typography at 8, where a planned headline-behind-the-ridge interlock was traded for legibility.

11. NO OTHER DEVIATIONS. No subagent stalled, no transient-error retry was needed, the window was never broadened, and the conflict-of-interest screen did not trigger. The one mechanical deviation is the image hosting swap in item 12.

12. IMAGE HOSTING SWAP. The inline base64 body measured 2,225,760 bytes, far over the 100 KB transport threshold, so the image in this email is served from the pushed branch at raw.githubusercontent.com instead of being embedded. Verified live at HTTP 200, image/png, 1,659,502 bytes, matching the local file exactly. If the branch is ever deleted the image in this email will break, so pull the PNG from the branch if you want a durable copy.

Sources

  • Alaska's News Source (KTUU/KTVA) — 2026-08-05 — PRIMARY SOURCE. Anchorage police seeking upgrades to real-time crime monitoring. INDEPENDENT of the subject. Carries the Aug 4 postponement, the debate, and both McCormick quotes.
  • Must Read Alaska — 2026 — Corroborator. Anchorage Assembly 2026 legislative priorities. INDEPENDENT of the subject. Confirms the RTCC programme and scale, does not reconstruct the Aug 4 debate.
  • MOA Public Health and Safety Committee packet — 2026 — Corroborator. Public Health and Safety Committee packet, item 7.07 Real-Time Crime Center. NOT INDEPENDENT (municipality's own document). Confirms the contract and system scope.
